The Real Food Revolution is Congressman Ryan's book discussing challenges in the food system, health impacts, and actionable steps for citizens.
Processed foods contribute significantly to rising rates of diabetes, heart disease, and cancer in the U.S. over the past 30 years.
Current agricultural subsidies primarily support crops used in highly processed foods like high-fructose corn syrup and soy oil.
Subsidizing unhealthy crops and later subsidizing healthcare for resulting diseases creates a financially unsustainable system.
Federal funding for healthcare programs like Medicare and Medicaid accounts for approximately one-third of the U.S. federal budget.

assumptions.text: Addressing food system reform is fiscally responsible and aligns with long-term budget sustainability goals.
Public health improvements through better food access can reduce national healthcare expenditures over time.
Grassroots mobilization and civic engagement can effectively counteract corporate lobbying influence in policymaking.
Consumers have the capacity and willingness to make healthier food choices when informed and provided accessible options.
Farmers can successfully transition to producing more fruits and vegetables if adequately supported with financial and infrastructural incentives.
Policy change is feasible within existing democratic structures if sustained pressure is applied by engaged citizen groups.
The current food system disproportionately harms low-income communities and children due to lack of access to nutritious food.
Healthcare reform cannot succeed without concurrent reform of foundational systems like agriculture and nutrition.
Elected officials respond to constituent demands when those demands are organized and persistent.
Agricultural innovation and localized food systems enhance environmental sustainability and community resilience.
